reference.source: Postgraduate Haematology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: An X-linked recessive deficiency of coagulation factor IX from mutations in F9, affecting mainly males with females usually carriers
The bleeding phenotype is clinically indistinguishable from haemophilia A, with haemarthroses, deep muscle bleeds and delayed post-traumatic or surgical bleeding
It cannot be separated from haemophilia A on clinical grounds or the screening coagulation tests alone; specific factor assays are required
The screening pattern is a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with normal prothrombin time and normal platelet count
A specific factor IX assay confirms the diagnosis and grades severity, and a normal factor VIII level distinguishes it from haemophilia A
Inhibitor (neutralising alloantibody) development is less common than in haemophilia A but can be associated with allergic or anaphylactic reactions to factor IX
Management uses factor IX replacement or non-factor haemostatic therapies and antifibrinolytics, with prophylaxis in severe disease to prevent joint damage
reference.pathophysiology: Haemophilia B is caused by mutations in F9 on the X chromosome that reduce the activity of coagulation factor IX, a vitamin K-dependent serine protease. Activated factor IX, with factor VIII as cofactor, forms the intrinsic tenase complex that activates factor X on the platelet surface. Deficiency of factor IX therefore impairs the same propagation step of coagulation as factor VIII deficiency, reducing thrombin generation and producing a slow, unstable clot. As in haemophilia A the initial platelet plug forms normally, so bleeding is delayed and occurs into joints and deep tissues, and recurrent haemarthroses drive progressive arthropathy.
additionalDifferentials: Other vitamin K-dependent factor deficiencies or warfarin effect
additionalInvestigations: Activated partial thromboplastin time, prothrombin time and platelet count
Mixing study to distinguish factor deficiency from an inhibitor
Factor IX activity assay to confirm diagnosis and grade severity
Factor VIII assay to differentiate from haemophilia A
Factor IX inhibitor assay when replacement response is poor
F9 genetic testing for diagnosis and carrier detection
redFlags: Intracranial haemorrhage, sometimes after minimal trauma
Compartment syndrome from an expanding muscle haematoma
Allergic or anaphylactic reactions accompanying inhibitor development against factor IX
reference.prognosis: With prophylaxis using factor IX or modern non-factor therapy, most patients have near-normal life expectancy and much reduced joint damage, though inhibitors, when they occur, can be complicated by allergic reactions and are harder to manage.
pitfalls: Assuming a haemophilia diagnosis is type A without a specific factor IX assay
Missing an inhibitor and its associated allergic reactions when replacement stops working
Attributing a low factor IX solely to vitamin K deficiency or anticoagulation without full assessment
Giving intramuscular injections that provoke deep bleeding
management: Prevent bleeds with prophylactic factor IX replacement and treat acute bleeds with factor IX concentrate; desmopressin has no role as it does not raise factor IX
Consider newer non-factor prophylaxis that rebalances haemostasis, such as the antithrombin-lowering short-interfering-RNA agent fitusiran, particularly where venous access is difficult
Offer adeno-associated-virus gene therapy in eligible adults to provide sustained endogenous factor IX
Add an antifibrinolytic such as tranexamic acid for mucosal and dental bleeding
Manage inhibitors with immune tolerance induction and bypassing agents, remaining alert to allergic and anaphylactic reactions to factor IX
Support joint health with physiotherapy and avoid intramuscular injections and NSAIDs
Monitor factor levels, screen for inhibitors, and assess joints, coordinating care through a haemophilia treatment centre
Provide genetic counselling and carrier testing for female relatives
